assumptions.assumption: Tier B (28-35 mph 'fast e-bike / scooter') is an e-bike-adjacent product with e-bike-like friction: no license, no plate, no insurance, no enforcement exposure. The four-tier plan implicitly treats the legal cliff as sitting between B and C.
assumptions.why_it_may_be_wrong: In California the cliff sits between A and B, not B and C. CVC 312.5 (verify) caps e-bikes at 750 W with Class 3 = pedal-assist-only to 28 mph and throttle to 20 mph. Anything with a throttle above 20 mph or any assist above 28 mph is a motorized bicycle / motor-driven cycle / motorcycle (CVC 406 / 405 / 400 - verify), which requires an M1 (M2 only for <=30 mph, <4 hp mopeds), DMV registration and a plate, and for motor-driven cycles/motorcycles proof of financial responsibility. SB 1271 (effective 2025) removed the 'switchable class' loophole and, from 1 Jan 2026, prohibits selling OR LEASING an e-bike or powered mobility device without UL 2849 / EN 15194 (bike) and UL 2271 (battery) certification - 'lease' plausibly captures HMP's rental and swap batteries. AB 1774 bans modifying to exceed class speed. 2025-26 follow-on bills gave police explicit authority to impound out-of-class devices for 48h+ (verify the bill number and LAPD/LASD operational policy). A courier on a 32 mph throttle 'e-bike' 8-10 hours a day is the highest-exposure rider on the road: no M license (CVC 12500), unregistered (CVC 4000(a)), uninsured (CVC 16028), impound plus ~$300+ release fees and 2-7 days of lost rental revenue per event. Net effect: the tiering collapses to two legal classes - (A) <=20 mph throttle / <=28 mph pedal-assist with no friction, and (B+C+D) M-license + plate + insurance - and tier B gets the worst of both: motorcycle-grade compliance cost at e-bike-grade rental price.
assumptions.magnitude: If the LA fleet plan is 40-60% tier B/C, roughly half the fleet carries a compliance burden the plan prices at zero. One impound per vehicle per year at ~$300 fees + 5 days downtime is ~10-15% of annual rental revenue on a $60/wk vehicle; a 20% impound rate per vehicle-year is a rounding error, a 100% rate is a business-model change. SB 1271 certification gaps on any non-UL swap battery SKU are a stop-ship for the swap product in LA.
assumptions.cheap_test: One day of desk work: read CVC 312.5, 406, 405, 400, 12500, 4000, 16028 and the DMV 'Motorcycles, Mopeds, and Scooters' page; pull the final chaptered text of SB 1271 and the 2025-26 impound bill; call LAPD Central Traffic Division and the Newton / Central area senior lead officers about e-bike/moped enforcement posture around Ceres Ave. Then spend two evenings in LA courier WhatsApp/Reddit/Facebook groups counting impound and citation reports by vehicle type. Ask the battery supplier for UL 2271 / UL 2849 certificates for every swap SKU.
assumptions.hmp_internal_data_needed: SF rental fleet (~100 vehicles) split by legal class (Class 1/2/3 vs motorized bicycle vs motor-driven cycle vs motorcycle); count of SF renter citations, impounds and DMV notices in the last 12 months by class; whether SF rental vehicles above 20 mph throttle are registered and plated today; UL certification status for each battery SKU in the ~300-subscriber swap program.

assumptions.assumption: The target LA courier holds, or will readily obtain, an M1/M2 license, so tiers B-D have the same addressable renter pool as tier A.
assumptions.why_it_may_be_wrong: The addressable LA two-wheel courier is disproportionately a recent immigrant without a California license; AB 60 licenses exist but require a separate M1/M2 written test plus skills test or CMSP course (verify whether AB 60 licenses can carry M endorsements), which costs weeks and a few hundred dollars that a rider choosing to rent rather than buy does not have. The NYC precedent is exactly this population: the great majority of moped-riding deliveristas were unlicensed and unregistered, and NYPD seized on the order of 10,000+ illegal mopeds in 2023-24 (verify count), not because riders were reckless but because the license/registration pathway did not fit them. Nothing in the LA plan changes that pathway. The founder's 'faster is better for LA' preference quietly assumes the licensed motorcyclist demographic, which is a car-owning commuter demographic, not a renter demographic.
assumptions.magnitude: If 50-80% of prospective LA renters lack an M license (NYC pattern), tiers B-D address 20-50% of the pool that tier A addresses, while carrying higher capex per unit. A 100-vehicle fleet planned at 60% tier B-D could see those units run at 30-50% utilization while tier A is sold out.
assumptions.cheap_test: Three dinner rushes at LA pickup hotspots (DTLA/Arts District, Koreatown, Hollywood, Westwood, Santa Monica): 10-minute intercept survey of 100 two-wheel couriers - what they ride, whether they hold a CA license and which class, whether they would rent, what weekly price. Compare with DMV Class M issuance counts for LA County (public data request). Cost: two people, three evenings, gift cards.
assumptions.hmp_internal_data_needed: For SF's ~100 renters and ~300 swap subscribers: license class on file at signup (or whether license class is even collected); share of SF FLASH / Lightning MK.II BUYERS who are couriers vs commuters; SF conversion from tier A rental to any faster tier.

assumptions.assumption: If an unlicensed renter crashes a 45 mph HMP moped, the exposure is the rider's (and the rider's platform insurance), not HMP's - so the rental operator can lease tiers B-D without verifying M licenses.
assumptions.why_it_may_be_wrong: CVC 14608 prohibits renting a motor vehicle to anyone not licensed for it and CVC 14609 (verify) requires inspecting and recording the license; violating a statutory standard raises a rebuttable presumption of negligence (negligence per se), which is the textbook negligent-entrustment fact pattern (CACI 724). The federal Graves Amendment shields rental companies only from vicarious liability, expressly not from negligent entrustment. Commercial liability policies for rental fleets typically exclude unlicensed operators, so the one claim that matters is the one that is not covered. DoorDash / Uber Eats occupational accident and third-party coverage attach to the courier while on an active delivery in the declared mode; a rider registered in 'bike' mode on a moped is arguably outside that coverage. A single serious pedestrian or rider injury at 45 mph in LA routinely settles above $1M - more than eight years of Ceres Ave rent - and the small-business owner is the deep pocket in the room.
assumptions.magnitude: Tail risk: one uninsured seven-figure claim ends the company. Expected value: if 100 tier B-D vehicles ride 300 days/yr, and serious-injury crashes run ~1 per 100,000-300,000 moped-miles (verify against CHP SWITRS), a 100-vehicle fleet at 60 mi/day sees 6-18 serious crashes per year - enough that 'we never had one in SF' is a small-sample artifact, not a risk estimate.
assumptions.cheap_test: Before signing: get 2-3 written quotes from specialty insurers (Zoomo's / Revel-style fleet programs, XInsurance, motorcycle rental carriers) for a fleet of registered mopeds/motorcycles rented to gig couriers, and ask explicitly (a) whether unlicensed-operator crashes are excluded, (b) the per-vehicle-month premium, (c) whether 'delivery use' is covered at all. Pay an LA insurance-defense attorney for one hour on CVC 14608/14609 and negligent entrustment as applied to gig-courier rentals. Pull SWITRS motorcycle/moped injury rates for LAPD Central and Newton areas.
assumptions.hmp_internal_data_needed: SF rental agreement text and the current SF policy: named carrier, covered vehicle classes, exclusions for unlicensed operators and commercial delivery use; the SF incident/claim log for rentals (all crashes, injuries, third-party demands) by vehicle class; whether SF verifies license class today and keeps CVC 14609-style records.

assumptions.assumption: Delivery platforms reward speed: a 40-50 mph vehicle in LA gets more and longer orders per hour than a 20 mph e-bike, which justifies a higher rental price ceiling for tiers C-D.
assumptions.why_it_may_be_wrong: Platforms dispatch by DECLARED mode, not actual speed. DoorDash 'bike' mode requires no license and is radius-limited to short-hop orders (typical ~2-3 miles - verify per market); 'scooter/motorcycle' mode requires a driver's license, and for motorcycles proof of insurance. Uber Eats 'scooter' mode requires a valid driver's license, a motorized scooter under 50cc equivalent, and state-minimum liability insurance; 'bicycle' mode needs only ID. So the rider who lacks an M license (assumption 2) can only monetize a moped in bike mode, where the app hands out e-bike-radius orders - the speed premium is never paid. The rider who IS licensed and insured can and often will declare 'car' or 'scooter' and is then competing with cars on long orders, not with e-bikes. Either way the incremental hourly earnings of tier C over tier A are far smaller than raw speed suggests, and the rental price ceiling for tier C converges toward tier A's ceiling. DoorDash's own 2025 claim that two-wheelers earn ~10% more per hour than cars is an argument for dense-area e-bikes, not for 45 mph mopeds in spread-out LA.
assumptions.magnitude: If tier C earns riders only +10-20% per hour over tier A rather than the +40-60% implied by speed, the sustainable weekly rental premium is ~$10-20, not ~$50-80 - which does not cover the extra ~$2,000-4,000 capex, registration and insurance per unit. Tiers C-D then cannot price above tier A and the fleet capex plan is wrong by roughly the tier C/D share.
assumptions.cheap_test: One week, two riders, one phone each: run a DoorDash and Uber Eats account in 'bike' mode on a tier A e-bike and another in 'scooter/motorcycle' mode on a FLASH from the Ceres Ave area; log every offer (distance, pay, accept/decline) and hourly net. Cross-check with screenshots from 10 LA couriers in each mode. Also read the current DoorDash and Uber Eats help pages on per-mode eligibility and any LA-specific mode availability.
assumptions.hmp_internal_data_needed: Self-reported weekly earnings and app mode for SF renters by vehicle model; SF rental price and utilization by tier (do SF couriers already pay a premium for FLASH over an e-bike?); SF renter churn by tier.

assumptions.assumption: Theft, crash damage and insurance on 40-70 mph vehicles scale only modestly with speed, so per-unit contribution margin holds across tiers.
assumptions.why_it_may_be_wrong: Three separate cost lines move against faster tiers. (1) Insurance: an unregistered e-bike fleet needs general liability only; a registered moped/motorcycle fleet rented to commercial couriers needs per-vehicle auto liability on a specialty program - historically the reason Revel exited moped sharing in NYC/SF/DC in late 2023 and Scoot's SF moped fleet shrank; realistic quotes may land at $60-200 per vehicle per month or be declined outright for 'delivery use' (verify with quotes). (2) Crash cost: kinetic energy scales with v^2, so a 45 mph crash carries ~5x the energy of a 20 mph one; write-off frequency, not just repair cost, rises. (3) Theft: LA e-scooter/e-moped theft rose sharply (LAPD data cited a 129% jump in an earlier period; e-bike theft up 25-40% YoY in LA per industry trackers) with 5-10% recovery; a plated, keyed moped with GPS/immobilizer may actually do better than an e-bike on theft, but the ~$4-8k replacement cost per loss is 3-4x higher. Ceres Ave sits between the Arts District and Skid Row in LAPD Central Area, a high-property-crime environment for overnight fleet storage.
assumptions.magnitude: If tier C rents for ~$250-300/month and insurance alone is $100-150/vehicle/month, insurance consumes 35-60% of revenue before depreciation, repairs and theft; a 5-8% annual fleet-value theft/total-loss rate on $6k units is another ~$30-40/vehicle/month. Combined, tier C/D contribution margin can go negative while tier A stays positive.
assumptions.cheap_test: Obtain the insurance quotes in assumption 3 (same phone calls). Pull LAPD Central and Newton area vehicle-theft and burglary counts around the 90021 zip from LAPD open data. Ask Zoomo or a former Revel/Scoot ops lead (LinkedIn cold message) for their per-vehicle insurance and loss rates. Price a GPS + immobilizer per unit.
assumptions.hmp_internal_data_needed: SF per-vehicle-month figures by model: theft/total-loss rate, repair cost per 1,000 miles, average crash repair bill, downtime days; current SF insurance premium per vehicle and what it actually covers; SF shop burglary/theft incidents.

assumptions.assumption: The SF battery-swap economics (~300 subscribers around one shop) carry over to 40-50 mph vehicles served from a single hub at 768 Ceres.
assumptions.why_it_may_be_wrong: Energy per mile rises roughly with v^2 (aero) so a 45 mph moped draws ~40-60 Wh/mile versus ~15-25 Wh/mile for a 20 mph e-bike (verify on HMP's own vehicles): 2-3x the Wh per delivery-mile on top of LA's longer average delivery distance. Either the vehicle carries a 2-3x larger (heavier, costlier, often non-swappable) pack, or the rider swaps 2-3x as often. The SF swap program works because subscribers work within a short ride of the shop; a single hub in the Arts District is 4-8 miles from Koreatown, Hollywood, Silver Lake, Westwood and Santa Monica, where LA's two-wheel order density is. A rider will not ride 6 miles each way mid-shift to swap; they will buy a bigger-battery vehicle and charge at home, which removes them from the swap revenue line entirely. Battery capex per active subscriber is therefore 2-3x SF's, cycle life is shorter at higher discharge rates, and the catchment shrinks to DTLA proper.
assumptions.magnitude: If swap capex per subscriber goes from ~1.5 packs to ~3-4 packs of larger capacity, battery capex per subscriber roughly triples; if the effective catchment is DTLA only, the LA subscriber ceiling in year one may be 50-100, not the 300 that SF suggests. That is a pricing or product change (larger packs, home charging, mobile swap van), not a hub-lease decision - but it removes the swap line from the Ceres Ave revenue stack.
assumptions.cheap_test: Instrument one vehicle from each tier with a Wh meter and ride representative LA delivery loops (DTLA, K-town, Hollywood) for a week; compute Wh/mile and swaps per 8-hour shift. Overlay a 3-mile radius from 768 Ceres on a heat map of restaurant density (Yelp/Google) and DoorDash 'busy' zones to size the true swap catchment.
assumptions.hmp_internal_data_needed: SF swap program: Wh/mile and swaps per week per subscriber by vehicle model; subscriber home/work distance from the shop and churn vs distance; battery cycle count at retirement by model; swap revenue vs battery capex per subscriber.

assumptions.assumption: E-moped and e-motorcycle riders are the same customer as e-bike renters, so LA courier demand can be served with a fleet weighted toward FLASH / Lightning-class vehicles - and 768 Ceres is where that customer works.
assumptions.why_it_may_be_wrong: Two conflated customers. HMP's FLASH / Lightning MK.II sales (>1,000 vehicles) skew toward commuters and car-replacement buyers who BUY; couriers who RENT are cash-constrained and choose the cheapest vehicle that clears the app and the law, which in California is a Class 2 e-bike. LA's courier base is also overwhelmingly car-based: DoorDash reports 72% of SF deliveries on two wheels but only ~30% in San Diego; LA is unpublished and plausibly at or below San Diego. The two-wheel minority is concentrated in dense pockets (DTLA, K-town, Hollywood, Westwood, Santa Monica/Venice) where a 20 mph e-bike already suffices - which is exactly why those couriers are on two wheels. So 'LA is spread out, therefore faster vehicles' has the causality backwards: spread-out LA is served by cars, and the two-wheel opportunity is the dense pockets, most of which are 4-8 miles from Ceres Ave. The founder's faster-vehicle preference matches the SF buyer, not the LA renter.
assumptions.magnitude: If LA two-wheel courier share is ~20-30% and tier C/D demand within it is <20%, the addressable tier C/D rental pool near Ceres Ave could be in the low dozens of riders, versus a plan sized for 100+ rental units. The site question and the fleet-mix question are the same question: the right fleet for a Ceres Ave hub may be tier A for DTLA, and the right site for tier A may not be Ceres Ave.
assumptions.cheap_test: Three dinner rushes counting vehicle type (car / e-bike / moped / motorcycle / other) at 5 LA hotspots; ask DoorDash's LA city team for their LA two-wheel share (they publish these for other cities); pull HMP's Shopify orders shipped to LA County zips by model and email those buyers a 3-question survey (courier vs commuter, would you rent, which tier).
assumptions.hmp_internal_data_needed: Shopify sales to LA County zips by model and buyer type; SF: share of FLASH / Lightning buyers who are couriers; share of SF couriers who rent tier A vs any faster tier; SF renter-to-buyer conversion by tier; SF rental waitlist by vehicle type.
